docs.title: JAX-Aero
docs.text:
A steady airfoil and wing solver in JAX: compressible Euler, laminar Navier-Stokes and Spalart-Allmaras RANS on structured grids, in 2D and, on single-block grids, in 3D, on CPU or GPU. Grids are generated round a single airfoil or a slat, main element and flap from their coordinates, or read from Plot3D and CGNS files with any number of blocks (3D: one Plot3D block). A case is two JSON files.

pip install jax-aero[plot,cgns]
jaxaero my_case --check     # build and draw the grid
jaxaero my_case             # solve
python -m jaxaero.polar my_case --alpha -2 10 1
  • Running a case
  • Your own airfoil
  • A multi-element airfoil
  • A 3D wing
  • Case reference
  • Equations and method
  • Developer guide and design notes

docs.title: Case reference
docs.text:
Generated from src/jaxaero/case/schema.py (python -m jaxaero.case --write); do not edit. How to write a case: the guide.

Every section may carry a "notes" string. Unknown keys are errors, a missing key takes its default, and an option that is not implemented is an error listing the alternatives.

docs.title: general
docs.text: key type default meaning case_name string required names the output directory description string case_name one line, printed in the log save_path string results output root, relative to the case directory

docs.title: domain
docs.text: key type default grids meaning grid string required all where the grid comes from: generated round one airfoil (o_grid, c_grid) or round a slat, main element and flap (multi_element), or read from a file; one of c_grid, file, multi_element, o_grid airfoil string required o_grid, c_grid naca + 4 digits (closed trailing edge; naca0012_blunt for the standard open one), or a coordinate file (Selig, Lednicer or two columns), scaled to unit chord cells_airfoil integer required o_grid, c_grid cells round the airfoil cells_wake integer required c_grid cells along each side of the wake cut cells_normal integer required o_grid, c_grid cells from the wall to the far field wall_spacing number required o_grid, c_grid, multi_element first-cell height, chords; for y+ ~ 1 see docs/own-airfoil.md trailing_edge string as_given o_grid, c_grid close closes an open trailing edge (needed for a C-grid); as_given keeps it, and an O-grid meshes its base; one of as_given, close far_field number 100.0 o_grid, c_grid, multi_element distance of the outer boundary from the airfoil, chords leading_edge_spacing number 0.002 o_grid, c_grid, multi_element surface cell length at the leading edge, chords trailing_edge_spacing number 0.002 o_grid, c_grid, multi_element surface cell length at the trailing edge, chords elements list [] multi_element the section, front to back: {"role": "slat"|"main"|"flap", "file": F} each (a coordinate file as for airfoil; leave file out when domain.file holds all the curves), as deployed; a slat or flap may add deflection_deg (further deployed from the given position: flap trailing edge down, slat leading edge down), gap (from the upstream trailing edge to the downstream element) and overlap (along the main element's chord, positive when the elements overlap) to be re-placed; docs/multi-element.md cells_per_chord integer required multi_element wall cells per unit length (more where the wall is clustered) layer_cells integer 32 multi_element cells across each element's near-wall layer layer_thickness number 0.02 multi_element near-wall layer thickness, chords; thinner in gaps and concave corners gap_cells integer 16 multi_element least cells across a gap between elements even_cells integer 4 multi_element every edge's cell count a multiple of this (4: two grid-sequencing levels) file string required file, multi_element the grid file: Plot3D (formatted or unformatted, either byte order, 2D or 3D, single- or multi-block, iblank, gzip) or CGNS in HDF5 storage (structured zones; pip install h5py); for multi_element, a file of curves holding every element (a point count, then the points, per curve; curves join into closed contours) format string auto file auto reads it from the contents; one of auto, cgns, plot3d coordinate_scale number 1.0 file, multi_element factor on every coordinate, to the length the Reynolds number is per (1/18 for a grid in inches with an 18 in chord) patches list [] file rules naming the boundary faces the file does not name, first match wins: {"name": N, "x_min": .., "x_max": .., "y_min": .., "y_max": ..} (3D grids: also z_min, z_max), every bound optional reference_length number 1.0 all length the force coefficients are per (3D: the moment's) reference_area number or null null all 3D grids (required there): area the force coefficients are per; 2D coefficients are per unit span moment_centre list [0.25, 0.0, 0.0] all point the pitching moment is about, [x, y] or [x, y, z]; nose-up positive about the spanwise axis (z in 2D, y in 3D)

docs.title: boundary_conditions
docs.text:
One entry per patch of the grid, "<patch>": {"type": ..., "model": ...}; a patch left out takes the default for its name (below).

key type default meaning type string required the condition; one of slip_wall, no_slip_wall, symmetry, far_field, inflow_total, outflow_static model string freestream far_field only: point_vortex adds the compressible vortex of the current lift at the quarter chord of the longest body, for a far field nearer than ~100 chords; one model per case; one of freestream, point_vortex type condition slip_wall inviscid wall (default wall when inviscid) no_slip_wall adiabatic no-slip wall (default wall when viscous) symmetry mirror plane far_field Riemann invariants against the freestream (default farfield) inflow_total subsonic inflow at the freestream total pressure and temperature, in its direction (default inflow) outflow_static subsonic outflow at the freestream static pressure (default outflow)

docs.title: freestream
docs.text: key type default meaning mach number required subsonic alpha_deg number 0.0 incidence, degrees reynolds number or null null per unit length of the grid (per chord for a grid of unit chord); null is inviscid temperature number absolute, in the unit of sutherland_temperature; Sutherland's law needs it

docs.title: material_properties
docs.text: key type default meaning specific_heat_ratio number 1.4 dynamic_viscosity string constant viscous cases only; one of constant, sutherland sutherland_temperature number 198.6 (R) or 110.3 (K) prandtl_number number 0.72 the one implemented

docs.title: turbulence
docs.text: key type default meaning model string none sa_noft2: Spalart-Allmaras without ft2, with SA-neg; one of none, sa_noft2 freestream_nu_tilde_ratio number 3.0 far-field nu~/nu (3 to 5)

docs.title: convective_fluxes
docs.text: key type default meaning riemann_solver string hllc one of hllc, roe limiter string minmod minmod where a shock may form; none for smooth flow (minmod stalls viscous convergence); van_albada for a shock with a boundary layer; one of minmod, none, van_albada muscl_kappa number 0.0 unlimited MUSCL family: 0 Fromm (the default), 1/3 third-order upwind-biased (CFL3D's default), -1 fully upwind; other than 0 only with limiter none

docs.title: time_integration
docs.text: key type default meaning solver string explicit explicit (multistage Runge-Kutta, local time step) or implicit (Newton-Krylov; use it for viscous cases); one of explicit, implicit rk_scheme string rk5_jameson explicit path; one of euler, rk4_jameson, rk5_jameson cfl number 1.5 explicit path

docs.title: implicit
docs.text: key type default meaning cfl number 10.0 starting CFL cfl_max number 1000.0 ceiling of the CFL ramp cfl_growth number 1.3 largest CFL growth per step cfl_cutback number 4.0 CFL divisor after a rejected step cfl_min number 0.5 CFL floor preconditioner string line_j one of line_j, none jacobian string first_order of the Krylov operator: first_order (defect correction) or exact; one of exact, first_order krylov_tol number 0.01 relative linear residual to reach krylov_subspace integer 10 GMRES vectors before a restart krylov_restarts integer 2 GMRES restarts krylov_success number 0.5 linear residual reduction for the CFL to grow max_relative_update number or null null bound on a step's relative change of density, pressure and nu~ (0.2 for SA at incidence)

docs.title: convergence
docs.text: key type default meaning max_iters integer 40000 iteration ceiling tol number 1e-12 residual drop from its running peak forces_tol number or null 0.0001 stop once CL, CD and CM each vary by less than this over the last quarter of the iterations (at least four blocks there); null: run to tol or max_iters grid_sequencing integer 0 solve first on this many coarser grids, each the next with every other node (cell counts, patch and interface limits must stay even), each to settled forces or max_iters, and start the next from it; 0: the grid only block_iters integer 200 explicit, 20 implicit iterations per device call; forces are monitored at this interval

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
Each layer only imports from the layers below it.

simulation.py, __main__.py   load a case, build the operator, iterate, write the result
polar.py      many angles at once: the step mapped over the freestream, split over GPUs
plot.py       figures from written results
case/         schema (every key, declared once), loader, domain (where the grid comes from)
io/           result files and provenance
post/         forces: Cp, Cf, CL, CD, CM, per body (2D and 3D)
solvers/      explicit (Runge-Kutta), implicit (Newton-Krylov), krylov (GMRES),
              preconditioners (line-implicit), driver (the iteration loop, batches, GPUs)
numerics/     residual, reconstruction, limiters, Riemann solvers, gradients,
              boundary conditions, SA source terms
physics/      Euler, Navier-Stokes and SA pointwise functions
mesh/         blocks and metrics (2D and 3D), meshes (patches, bodies, wall distance),
              the atlas (all blocks packed into one array; atlas3d: one 3D block),
              Plot3D and CGNS readers, assembly (interfaces and patch names; assemble3d),
              3D sides (block3d: rectangles, O seams, poles), grid generation, quality,
              coarsening (grid sequencing: every other node, the solution carried back)
geometry/     airfoil coordinates: file readers, NACA 4-digit, splines
core/         state, configuration, constants, linear algebra (block-tridiagonal:
              cyclic reduction, Thomas as its reference)

docs.title: Dimensions
docs.text: One code for 2D and 3D: the dimension d is the grid's (Grid.dim). State rows come from core.state.Rows(d); physics takes a velocity vector and a normal (d, ...); the residual loops over the d face families (Grid.faces). Write new numerics that way: never u, v or sx, sy outside 2D-only code (generators, plots). The 2D named views of a Grid (x_node, area, sx_i, ...) exist for that 2D-only code. tests/verification/test_extruded.py checks that the 3D operator contains the 2D one.

docs.title: Adding a scheme, a boundary condition or a key
docs.text:
Interchangeable pieces live in registries: dictionaries from the name used in the case files to a function. They are looked up before tracing, so jitted code never branches on a string. To add one, write the function, add it to the registry, and if it needs a new case key, add one line to case/schema.py. Then regenerate the case reference with python -m jaxaero.case --write (a test fails if you forget).

registry entries fluxes, numerics/riemann.py hllc (default), roe limiters, numerics/limiters.py minmod (default), van_albada, none Runge-Kutta schemes, solvers/explicit.py euler, rk4_jameson, rk5_jameson (default) preconditioners, solvers/preconditioners.py line_j (default), none grid sources, case/domain.py o_grid, c_grid, file boundary conditions, numerics/boundary.py slip_wall, no_slip_wall, symmetry, far_field, inflow_total, outflow_static far-field models, numerics/boundary.py freestream (default), point_vortex

The reasons behind the defaults, and the alternatives that were tried and dropped, are in the design notes. Read them before changing a default.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu python -m pytest tests -q -m "not slow"   # about 400 tests, 5 minutes
JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu python -m pytest tests -q -m slow         # manufactured solutions, batched polars, 17 minutes
  • tests/unit/: each piece on its own (fluxes, limiters, boundary conditions, grid generation and readers, viscous terms, SA terms, GMRES, preconditioners, the driver, the schema).
  • tests/verification/: metric identities, freestream preservation, the implicit path, the Navier-Stokes manufactured solution, batched polars against single runs.
  • tests/validation/: the validation scripts.

Tests that need downloaded grids skip when data/grids is missing. Run python validation/grids/make_grids.py once to write the grids the validation tests generate themselves.

Comparisons with published data are in validation/ (python validation/validate.py --suite rans), with figures in validation/gallery/.

docs.title: Running a case
docs.text: A case is a directory with two files, following JAX-Fluids: case.json describes the problem (grid, freestream, gas, turbulence model, boundary conditions) and numerical.json the method (flux, limiter, solver, iterations). Every key is listed in the case reference. To set up your own geometry, see your own airfoil, a multi-element airfoil or a 3D wing.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
example flow grid naca0012_euler Euler, M 0.8, 1.25 deg generated O-grid naca0012_laminar laminar, M 0.5, 1 deg, Re 5000 generated C-grid clarky_sa SA RANS, M 0.2, 4 deg, Re 3e6 C-grid round a downloaded coordinate file naca0012_sa SA RANS, M 0.15, 10 deg, Re 6e6 NASA TMR C-grid from file rae2822_transonic_sa transonic SA RANS, M 0.729, 2.31 deg, Re 6.5e6 NASA NPARC C-grid from file flatplate_sa SA RANS boundary layer, M 0.2, Re 5e6 NASA TMR flat-plate grid 30p30n_sa three-element high lift, M 0.17, 5.5 deg, Re 1.71e6 JAXA 117-block grid from file main_flap_sa two-element high lift (30P30N main and flap), M 0.17, 5.5 deg, Re 1.71e6 generated multi-element grid

The grids read from files are not in the repository; data/grids/README.md says where to download each. The first three examples and main_flap_sa need nothing else.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
jaxaero examples/naca0012_euler              # or: python -m jaxaero examples/naca0012_euler
jaxaero examples/naca0012_euler --check      # build and draw the grid, do not solve
jaxaero examples/naca0012_sa --set case.freestream.alpha_deg=12
jaxaero my_case --out /scratch/me/run1 --quiet

--set file.section.key=value changes one key for this run, and can be repeated. From Python:

from jaxaero import load_case, run

case = load_case("examples/naca0012_sa", overrides=("case.freestream.alpha_deg=12",))
result = run(case)
result.write()
print(result.forces.cl, result.forces.cd, result.history.orders_dropped)

The validation cases in validation/cases/ run the same way.

A run stops at the first of: its forces settled (settled: CL, CD and CM each vary by less than convergence.forces_tol, 1e-4, over the last quarter of the iterations), the residual down by tol from its peak (converged), or max_iters. It also stops, as stalled, if a whole block of iterations left the state unchanged (every step rejected), and as non_finite on a NaN. convergence.grid_sequencing = n solves first on the grid coarsened n times (every other node each time) and starts each finer grid from the coarser solution: fewer iterations on a fine grid. Every block's cell counts and patch and interface limits must stay even (JAXA's 30P30N grids, for one, are refused at the start). Polars (below) run every angle to tol or max_iters, on the case's grid only.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Results go to <case>/results/<case_name>/, or to --out:

file content *_fields.npz the solution U and the grid nodes, per block *_surface.dat x, Cp and Cf on every wall face; with several bodies also y and a body column *_residual.dat, *_lift.dat convergence histories *_metadata.json forces, convergence, the case files as run, git hash, versions, device

python -m jaxaero.plot <result dir> writes figures to figures/ there: Mach and Cp fields, wall Cp and Cf, convergence. It only reads these files, so you can plot results copied back from a cluster without a GPU.

U is conservative, (rho, rho u, rho v, E), plus rho nu~ / nu_inf with SA. Everything is nondimensional, based on freestream density, freestream speed of sound and the chord, so the freestream is rho = 1, (u, v) = M (cos a, sin a), p = 1/gamma.

docs.title: Polars
docs.text:
python -m jaxaero.polar examples/rae2822_transonic_sa --alpha -2 5.5 0.5

--alpha takes start, stop and step. All the angles run together as one batch, split over every visible GPU. The output is polar.dat (one row per angle), polar_metadata.json and a normal result directory per angle.

docs.title: Boundary conditions
docs.text:
Every grid has named patches on its boundaries, and boundary_conditions gives each one a type:

"boundary_conditions": {
    "wall": {"type": "no_slip_wall"},
    "farfield": {"type": "far_field", "model": "point_vortex"}
}

The types are slip_wall, no_slip_wall (adiabatic), symmetry, far_field (characteristic; model is freestream or point_vortex), inflow_total and outflow_static.

A patch you leave out gets the default for its name: wall is no-slip in a viscous case and slip otherwise, farfield is far_field, symmetry is symmetry, inflow is inflow_total, outflow is outflow_static. Any other name must be given a type.

Where the patch names come from:

  • Generated grids have wall and farfield.
  • CGNS files: the family name of each boundary, else its BC type (BCWall* is wall, BCFarfield is farfield, and so on), else the name of the BC node.
  • Faces a file does not name (all of them, in Plot3D) are named by domain.patches box rules if you give any, else by the loop they lie on: the outer boundary is farfield, each body is wall.

Block interfaces, the seam of an O-grid and the wake cut of a C-grid are found from coincident faces. They are not patches, and you never declare them.

CGNS files in the older ADF format are refused. Convert them with the CGNS tools: adf2hdf in.cgns out.cgns.

docs.title: A multi-element airfoil
docs.text: For a slat, main element and flap the solver can generate the grid ("grid": "multi_element", below); for any other geometry with coves and gaps, make a structured multi-block grid with your mesher and point the case at the file. The worked example is examples/30p30n_sa: the 30P30N three-element airfoil on JAXA's 117-block grid (download instructions in data/grids/README.md).

docs.title: 1. What the grid file must be
docs.text:
• Format: Plot3D (any variant: formatted or binary, single or double precision, 2D, or 3D with one plane used) or CGNS saved in HDF5. Pointwise, ICEM CFD and most structured meshers write one of these.
  • Blocks meet node to node. Interfaces are found by matching coincident block faces, so no connectivity file is needed, but the nodes on both sides of an interface must coincide. Non-matching (patched) interfaces are not supported.
  • Every wall closes round its body, and the outer boundary closes round everything.

In a CGNS file, boundary names come from the file (family names, else BC types). Plot3D has no names, so faces that are not interfaces are named by the loop they lie on: the outer loop becomes farfield, and each closed loop round a body becomes wall. For other cases, such as a symmetry plane, an inflow or an outflow, name faces with box rules in domain.patches (the flat-plate example does this).

docs.title: 2. case.json
docs.text:
{
    "general": {"case_name": "30p30n_sa"},
    "domain": {
        "grid": "file",
        "file": "data/grids/2Ddomain_L1_coarse_r1.p3d",
        "coordinate_scale": 0.05555555555555555
    },
    "freestream": {"mach": 0.17, "alpha_deg": 5.5, "reynolds": 1.71e6, "temperature": 295.56},
    "material_properties": {"dynamic_viscosity": "sutherland", "sutherland_temperature": 110.4},
    "turbulence": {"model": "sa_noft2"}
}

Units. The solver works in the length your Reynolds number is based on, and the force coefficients use the same length. JAXA's grid is in inches, with an 18 inch stowed chord, so coordinate_scale is 1/18. If your grid is already in chords, leave it out. If you would rather keep the grid as it is and quote coefficients per some other length, set reference_length; the Reynolds number is then per that length too.

The pitching moment is taken about (0.25, 0) in the scaled coordinates.

docs.title: 3. Check the grid
docs.text:
jaxaero examples/30p30n_sa --check

grid file 2Ddomain_L1_coarse_r1.p3d: 117 block(s), 63957 cells, 3 body(ies); implicit, hllc, limiter van_albada
grid quality: 63957 cells, min area 8.64e-10, min angle 34.4 deg, max growth 2.16, ...; far field >= 97.6 from the walls
  warning: neighbouring cells growing by up to 2.16x (over 1.5)
patch 'wall': no_slip_wall, 610 faces
patch 'farfield': far_field, 560 faces
body 0: x -0.0848 to 0.0188, y -0.1162 to 0.0066, 266 wall faces
body 1: x 0.0438 to 0.8741, y -0.0546 to 0.0619, 254 wall faces
body 2: x 0.8714 to 1.1307, y -0.1460 to 0.0218, 90 wall faces

Look at three things. The number of bodies should be the number of elements: if it is lower, a wall did not close, usually because two blocks meet with nodes that do not coincide. The body extents should be in chords. And grid.png should show every element outlined in its own colour:

Bodies are numbered by their leading edge, from the front: here slat 0, main 1, flap 2.

docs.title: 4. Run
docs.text:
jaxaero examples/30p30n_sa

Use the implicit solver with van_albada; high-lift flows at low Mach number converge slowly, so give it several thousand iterations (8000 here). The coarsest 30P30N level (63,957 cells) runs its 8000 iterations in 7 minutes on an A100 (49 ms each); its forces keep moving by a little more than the forces_tol bar, so it does not stop earlier. On a small GPU, run a grid of this size on a cluster instead. Its block sizes are odd, so grid_sequencing refuses it.

The forces are printed for the whole configuration and for each body. On this coarsest level, at 5.5 degrees:

CL CD slat (body 0) 0.151 -0.065 main (body 1) 2.183 -0.135 flap (body 2) 0.453 0.259 total 2.787 0.059 JAXA's RANS, for comparison 2.877 0.040

On the third grid level (261 thousand cells) the lift comes within 0.03 % of JAXA's. Per-element drag is the difference of large pressure forces and depends strongly on the grid.

*_surface.dat lists Cp and Cf body by body, each starting from its trailing edge, with a body column to tell them apart.

docs.title: When the grid is refused
docs.text:
• a face coincides with more than one other face: two blocks overlap, or a block is duplicated in the file.
  • block k folds over: that block has cells of both orientations; fix it in the mesher.
  • no boundary condition for patch(es) [...]: the file names a boundary the case does not mention, and the name has no default. Add it to boundary_conditions; the message lists the grid's patch names.
  • a 1-to-1 interface the file declares is not matched: a CGNS file says two faces connect, but their nodes do not coincide.

docs.title: Generated grids
docs.text: "grid": "multi_element" builds the multi-block grid of a slat, main element and flap from their coordinates alone, in about a minute on a CPU. The examples are examples/main_flap_sa (the 30P30N without its slat, one file per element) and validation/cases/gen_30p30n_a5p5 (the full 30P30N from one curve file).

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text:
• The arrangement: a main element with a flap behind it, a slat ahead of it, or both (main+flap, slat+main, slat+main+flap, listed front to back), each trailing edge over the nose of the element behind it, as deployed in a single-slotted high-lift section. Not covered: two slats or two flaps (double- and triple-slotted systems), Krueger flaps, vanes, tabs, or elements side by side; for those, mesh with your own tool and use "grid": "file".
  • Each element a closed contour that does not cross itself or another element. Sharp or blunt trailing edges (a blunt base of any thickness), smooth or stepped coves, a cusp on the slat: all taken.
  • Gaps wide enough for the near-wall layers: each layer is at least 1.5 wall_spacing x layer_cells thick and at most 0.3 of the distance to the nearest other element, so a gap needs at least 5 wall_spacing x layer_cells (0.24 % of the chord at the defaults, 1.5e-5 and 32).
  • Units: coordinates in the length the Reynolds number is per, the section between 0.1 and 10 of it along x; otherwise set coordinate_scale.
  • Settings measured to build (round the 30P30N's, below): flap deflection 20 to 40 deg, gap 0.5 to 3 % of the chord, overlap -1 to +0.14 % (+2 % with a 3 % gap); slat deflection 20 to 30 deg, gap 1.5 to 4 %.

Outside these the grid is refused with the reason (below), never built folded.

docs.title: The coordinate files
docs.text:
Either one file per element (elements[k].file), in any format airfoil takes:

30P30N flap element          <- an optional name line
1.1278162  -0.1459988        <- x y, one point per line, round the contour
1.1253447  -0.1449002
...

Selig (round the contour, starting at a trailing-edge point), Lednicer (the two point counts, then the upper and the lower surface from the leading edge) or a plain two-column table, in either direction. A blunt trailing edge is left open: the file runs from one end of the base round to the other, and the base is the straight line between them.

Or one curve file for all elements (domain.file, elements then roles only):

33                           <- a curve: its point count,
15.730081  0.551473  0.0     <- then its points, x y (a third column is ignored)
...
9                            <- the next curve
...

Curves join end to end, in any order and direction, into closed contours, one per element; the elements are taken front to back by their leading edges. A blunt base is its own curve (or part of one); it is found as the straight piece between the two sharpest corners at the trailing edge.

In both, the elements are as deployed, in one frame, x downstream and y up. Corners (points where the contour turns more than 30 deg: a cove step, a cusp, a base's corners) are kept as nodes, the surface is splined between them, so give the corners as points of the file. A slat or flap may be re-placed instead of re-drawn (deflection_deg, gap, overlap below).

docs.title: Case keys
docs.text:
"domain": {
    "grid": "multi_element",
    "elements": [{"role": "main", "file": "main.dat"},
                 {"role": "flap", "file": "flap.dat", "deflection_deg": 5.0, "gap": 0.015}],
    "wall_spacing": 1.5e-05,
    "cells_per_chord": 150
}
  • Re-placing a slat or flap: deflection_deg rotates it further deployed from its given position (flap trailing edge down about its leading edge, slat leading edge down about its trailing edge), then gap (from the upstream trailing edge to the downstream element) and overlap (along the main element's chord, positive when they overlap) set its position; leave either out to keep it. The main element stays where it is.
  • Resolution: cells_per_chord on the walls (clustered at edges and corners), wall_spacing for the first cell (1.5e-5 chords is y+ ~ 1 at Re 1.71e6), layer_cells and layer_thickness for each element's near-wall layer (thinner in gaps and coves), gap_cells across a gap at least. Every block's cell counts are multiples of even_cells (4: two grid-sequencing levels). Every key: the case reference.

Start high-lift cases from freestream (grid_sequencing 0): coarsened 30P30N grids settle on a separated flow (CL 1.5-1.6, CD 0.3-0.4) that the fine grid then takes thousands of iterations to wash out.

docs.title: What is built
docs.text: Each element has a near-wall layer, j from its wall; a front block wraps the first element's nose, a block runs over the first element and its wake, a slot block over each downstream element under the upstream wake (its left side the gap), a cove block in each cove, and blocks under the elements, split at each cove lip; a ring carries the grid to far_field. python scripts/plot_blocks.py CASE --window x0 x1 y0 y1 draws the blocks.

docs.title: When the grid is refused
docs.text: message meaning no multi-element template for elements [...] roles not in one of the three orders, front to back the section spans ... along x coordinates in another unit: set coordinate_scale ... near-wall layer would be ... thick ...: too thin a gap narrower than the layers need: lower wall_spacing x layer_cells, or open the gap ... outside the template's envelope: its landmarks lie in the order ... the elements are not arranged as the template expects (an element not behind the one before it, a cove where none can be) placing the flap: a gap of ... is out of reach at an overlap of ... the asked gap and overlap cannot both hold; the message gives the smallest gap there block 'cove2' folds a setting past the envelope (a flap overlapping by 2 % of the chord or more under a narrow gap)

docs.title: Quality and runs
docs.text:
On the 30P30N at 150 cells per chord (113k cells): no folded cell; the first cell within 1 % of wall_spacing and the walls orthogonal to 0.05 deg away from the trailing-edge and corner fans; cells as skewed as 13 deg where the main element's cove narrows into the flap gap; neighbouring cells across block interfaces within 1.4x of each other (median), up to 23x at the main element's cove corner. NACA-based sections (sharp and blunt trailing edges, a stepped and a smooth cove, a slat ahead of a plain main element: tests/verification/test_highlift_shapes.py) build with no cell skewed under 21 deg.

main_flap_sa (113k cells) settles at 0, 5.5 and 9.5 deg in 3760, 3560 and 6940 iterations (3.4 to 3.8 orders), CL 2.135, 2.803, 3.041, 116 ms an iteration on a V100. The generated 30P30N at 5.5 deg: CL 2.535, 2.808, 2.846 on 75k, 113k and 165k cells, its Cp on JAXA's RANS on all three elements (validation/compare_30p30n.py); this code on JAXA's grids: 2.787 on 64k cells, 2.8756 on 261k.

The settings round the 30P30N's (validation/highlift_envelope.py): every flap deflection from 20 to 40 deg with gaps 0.5 to 3 % and overlaps -1 to +0.14 % builds (but a 0.5 % gap, out of reach at -1 % overlap), and +2 % with a 3 % gap; a 2 % overlap under a narrower gap folds the cove block and is refused. Every slat deflection from 20 to 30 deg with gaps 1.5 to 4 % builds (under 2.4 % the overlap must come to -1 %: at its given -2.4 % the slat cannot come nearer).

docs.title: Your own airfoil
docs.text: This page takes a coordinate file you downloaded or exported and runs it. The worked example is examples/clarky_sa: the Clark Y file from the UIUC database, used exactly as downloaded.

docs.title: 1. The coordinate file
docs.text:
Put the file in a new directory, next to where case.json will go:

my_airfoil/
    clarky.dat
    case.json
    numerical.json

The reader accepts the usual formats:

  • Selig: a name line, then x y pairs going round the airfoil.
  • Lednicer: a name line, a line with the point counts of the two surfaces, then the upper and the lower surface, each from the leading edge.
  • Plain: two columns, no header.

Either direction round the contour is fine, and commas are read as spaces. The airfoil is scaled to unit chord, with its leading edge at the origin. That way a file in millimetres or a file offset from the origin give the same grid and the same coefficients as one in chords. Nothing is rotated: set the incidence with alpha_deg.

Most downloaded files have a slightly open trailing edge (0.1 to 0.3 % of the chord). A C-grid needs a sharp one, so add "trailing_edge": "close". This moves each surface by a small amount that grows linearly from zero at the leading edge to half the gap at the trailing edge. If you want to keep the blunt base, use an O-grid instead.

docs.title: 2. case.json
docs.text:
{
    "general": {"case_name": "clarky_sa"},
    "domain": {
        "grid": "c_grid",
        "airfoil": "clarky.dat",
        "trailing_edge": "close",
        "cells_airfoil": 256,
        "cells_wake": 64,
        "cells_normal": 96,
        "wall_spacing": 5e-6
    },
    "freestream": {"mach": 0.2, "alpha_deg": 4.0, "reynolds": 3e6, "temperature": 288.15},
    "material_properties": {"dynamic_viscosity": "sutherland", "sutherland_temperature": 110.4},
    "turbulence": {"model": "sa_noft2"}
}

The generated grid has two patches, wall and farfield. With a Reynolds number set, the wall defaults to no-slip and the far field to the characteristic condition, so boundary_conditions can be left out.

Which grid. A C-grid for viscous flow round a sharp trailing edge; an O-grid for inviscid flow, or to keep a blunt trailing edge.

How many cells. For RANS, 256 round the airfoil, 64 along the wake and 96 to 128 outward is a reasonable first grid (40 to 50 thousand cells). Double cells_airfoil, cells_wake and cells_normal and halve wall_spacing to see how much the answer still depends on the grid.

Wall spacing. For RANS the first cell should sit at y+ of about 1. A flat plate estimate, in chords:

re = 3e6
cf = 0.026 / re ** (1 / 7)                  # turbulent flat plate skin friction
wall_spacing = 1 / (re * (cf / 2) ** 0.5) / 2   # y+ = 1, halved for the suction peak
print(wall_spacing)                         # 4.3e-06

For laminar flow it is the boundary layer you need to resolve: aim for about 30 cells across it (the laminar example uses 1e-4 at Re 5000).

Far field. The default of 100 chords is safe. To bring it closer, add the point-vortex correction, which accounts for the lift's far-field signature: "boundary_conditions": {"farfield": {"type": "far_field", "model": "point_vortex"}}. The RAE 2822 validation grid uses it with its boundary 20 to 38 chords away.

docs.title: 3. numerical.json
docs.text:
{
    "convective_fluxes": {"limiter": "none"},
    "time_integration": {"solver": "implicit"},
    "implicit": {"max_relative_update": 0.2},
    "convergence": {"max_iters": 3000}
}

Use the implicit solver for any viscous case. The limiter: none for subsonic flow without shocks, van_albada for transonic RANS or high lift, minmod for inviscid shocks. max_relative_update keeps the first few hundred SA steps from overshooting.

docs.title: 4. Check the grid, then run
docs.text:
jaxaero my_airfoil --check

This builds the grid, prints the quality report and the patches, and writes results/clarky_sa/grid.png. It does not solve anything. For the Clark Y:

grid c_grid round clarky.dat: 256 + 2x64 wake x 96 cells, wall spacing 5e-06, far field 100; trailing-edge gap 0.0012 closed: ...
grid quality: 36864 cells, min area 9.74e-09, min angle 86.7 deg, max growth 1.24, max aspect 2.61e+06; wall: first cell 4.72e-06..5.11e-06, within 3.1 deg of orthogonal; far field >= 99.8 from the walls
patch 'wall': no_slip_wall, 256 faces
patch 'farfield': far_field, 576 faces
body 0: x -0.0000 to 1.0000, y -0.0302 to 0.0914, 256 wall faces

A grid with folded cells (negative area) is refused. Warnings follow the report when cells are skewed below 20 degrees or grow by more than 1.5 between neighbours. These are worth fixing, usually with more cells or a smaller leading_edge_spacing / trailing_edge_spacing, but the case still runs.

Then run it:

jaxaero my_airfoil
python -m jaxaero.plot my_airfoil/results/clarky_sa

On a 4 GB laptop GPU the Clark Y takes 6 minutes (0.29 s per iteration; an A100 is several times faster). It stops after 1160 iterations, once the forces have settled:

settled after 1160 iterations, residual peak 1.704433e-05 -> 6.698344e-09 (3.41 orders from peak)
CL = +0.801215   CD = +0.011022 (friction +0.007529)   CM = -0.075400

The drag is for a fully turbulent boundary layer: SA has no transition model, so expect more drag than a wind tunnel at this Reynolds number.

The small bumps near the leading edge are in the coordinate file, not the flow. The file has 61 points per surface with four or five digits, and its curvature jumps between neighbouring points (on the upper surface at x/c 0.02, 0.08 and 0.16). The solver follows the geometry it is given. If you see this in your own results, use a file with more points, or smooth it before running.

docs.title: 5. Is it converged?
docs.text: The forces are printed every block, and the log ends with the reason the run stopped and the orders the residual dropped from its peak. A run whose forces have settled (CL, CD and CM each moving less than convergence.forces_tol, 1e-4, over the last quarter of the iterations) stops by itself and says settled; the residual has then usually dropped three to five orders, and the forces would not change in the digits shown if you went on. A smaller forces_tol asks for more digits; null turns the test off and runs to tol or max_iters. A run that ends at max_iters has not settled: raise max_iters first. A residual stuck at two or three orders with an oscillating CL usually means a separated or unsteady flow, or a grid that is too coarse at the trailing edge.

docs.title: 6. A polar
docs.text:
python -m jaxaero.polar my_airfoil --alpha -4 12 2

This runs every angle together (on a GPU, as one batch) and writes polar.dat, with one row per angle: alpha, CL, CD, friction drag, CM, the orders the residual dropped, the iterations, the spread of CL over the last quarter of the run, and whether that spread is small enough to call CL settled. python -m jaxaero.plot on the polar directory draws it. Near and past stall, look at the settled column: a steady solver cannot settle a flow that is really unsteady.

docs.title: Changing one thing without editing the files
docs.text:
jaxaero my_airfoil --set case.freestream.alpha_deg=8 --set case.domain.cells_normal=128

The changed values are saved with the result.

docs.title: Equations
docs.text:
d/dt ∫ U dV + ∮ (F(U) - F_v(U, ∇U)) · n dS = 0,     U = (ρ, ρu, ρv, E)
F · n   = ( ρVn,  ρu Vn + p nx,  ρv Vn + p ny,  (E + p) Vn ),   Vn = u nx + v ny
F_v · n = ( 0,  (τ·n)x,  (τ·n)y,  (τ·V)·n + k ∇T·n )
τ = μ(∇V + ∇Vᵀ - ⅔(∇·V) I),   k = μ / (Pr (γ-1)),   T = a² = γp/ρ

Variables are scaled by the freestream density, the freestream speed of sound and the chord: the freestream is ρ = 1, (u, v) = M∞ (cos α, sin α), p = 1/γ, and μ = M∞/Re. Viscosity is constant or follows Sutherland's law, μ/μ∞ = T^{3/2} (1+s)/(T+s), s = S/T∞.

With Spalart-Allmaras (SA-noft2 with SA-neg, as defined by NASA's Turbulence Modeling Resource) a fifth equation is solved for ρν̃, stored over ν∞ so that it is O(1) beside the flow variables; the stresses and heat flux use μ + μ_t and μ/Pr + μ_t/Pr_t, μ_t = ρν̃ f_v1, Pr_t = 0.9:

∂(ρν̃)/∂t + ∇·(ρVν̃) = ρ c_b1 S̃ ν̃ − ρ c_w1 f_w (ν̃/d)² + (1/σ)[∇·((μ + ρν̃ f_n)∇ν̃) + c_b2 ρ|∇ν̃|²]

docs.title: Discretization
docs.text:
• Cell-centred finite volume on structured blocks. Every grid, single- or multi-block, is packed into one array (the atlas) with two ghost layers per block; ghost cells hold the neighbouring block's cells across an interface and the boundary condition's state on a patch.
  • Convective flux: MUSCL reconstruction of primitive variables from raw index differences, limited by minmod, van_albada or none; then HLLC (default) or Roe at each face.
  • Viscous flux: face gradients by the diamond construction, exact for a linear field on any quadrilateral.
  • Boundary conditions by patch: slip and adiabatic no-slip walls, symmetry, a characteristic far field (Riemann invariants, optionally against the freestream plus the compressible point vortex of the current lift), total-condition inflow and static-pressure outflow.

docs.title: Iteration to steady state
docs.text:
• Explicit: Jameson's multistage Runge-Kutta with local time steps.
  • Implicit: pseudo-transient Newton-Krylov. Each step solves (V/Δt + ∂R/∂U) ΔU = -R by right-preconditioned restarted GMRES on Jacobian-vector products from jax.linearize; by default the operator is the first-order residual's Jacobian (defect correction). The CFL grows by the residual reduction when the linear solve succeeded and is cut back after a rejected step. The preconditioner solves block-tridiagonal systems exactly along grid lines in j, through a C-grid's wake cut, with a first-order upwind approximate Jacobian (Mavriplis, AIAA J. 37 (1999)).

Both paths drive the same residual through the same on-device loop, so they share their converged solutions. A polar maps the step over the freestream and runs every angle at once, split over GPUs.

docs.title: Grids
docs.text: Generated round one airfoil by hyperbolic marching (Steger and Chaussee): O-grids and C-grids, Vinokur spacing along the surface and geometric growth off it. Or read from Plot3D or CGNS (HDF5), with block interfaces found from coincident faces and boundary patches named from the file or from geometric rules. Every grid passes a quality report before it runs.

docs.title: A 3D wing
docs.text: The solver runs 3D grids with the same two JSON files as 2D: the dimension is the grid's. It does not generate 3D grids: make a structured grid with your mesher and point the case at the file. The worked example is examples/onera_m6_sa, the ONERA M6 wing at NASA's Turbulence Modeling Resource conditions (case 2308), on a small grid that ships with the example.

docs.title: 1. What the grid file must be
docs.text:
• Format: Plot3D with three index directions (formatted or binary, single or double precision). CGNS is read in 2D only for now.
  • One block. Multi-block 3D grids are not supported yet.
  • What lies on each of its six sides is found from the coordinates:
    • two opposite sides whose nodes coincide become an interface (the seam of an O-grid round the wing section);
    • a side collapsed to a line (every face of zero area) becomes a pole, provided it lies round a seam direction with an even number of cells. The rounded tip of the example grid closes this way;
    • every other face is named by the box rules of domain.patches (section 2).
  • Axes: x along the chord, y along the span, z up. The angle of attack turns the freestream in the x-z plane.
  • The wall-normal index should be j. The implicit solver's preconditioner solves along j lines, which is what makes thin wall cells affordable. A wall on another index has not been tested.
  • A block that is left-handed is reversed in k on reading. A folded grid (a cell of non-positive volume) is refused.

A half model with the root on a symmetry plane, as in the example, is the usual set-up.

docs.title: 2. case.json
docs.text:
{
    "general": {"case_name": "onera_m6_sa"},
    "domain": {
        "grid": "file",
        "file": "om6_strct_16x44x24.ufmt",
        "patches": [
            {"name": "symmetry", "y_max": 1e-9},
            {"name": "wall", "x_min": -1.0, "x_max": 3.0, "y_max": 3.0, "z_min": -1.0, "z_max": 1.0},
            {"name": "farfield"}
        ],
        "reference_area": 1.15315084119,
        "reference_length": 0.8016729585,
        "moment_centre": [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
    },
    "boundary_conditions": {
        "wall": {"type": "no_slip_wall"},
        "farfield": {"type": "far_field"},
        "symmetry": {"type": "symmetry"}
    },
    "freestream": {"mach": 0.84, "alpha_deg": 3.06, "reynolds": 14.6e6, "temperature": 540.0},
    "material_properties": {"dynamic_viscosity": "sutherland", "sutherland_temperature": 198.6},
    "turbulence": {"model": "sa_noft2"}
}

Patches. A Plot3D file has no boundary names, so each boundary face takes the name of the first rule whose box contains its midpoint; a bound left out is unbounded. Here the root plane y = 0 is symmetry, the faces inside a box round the wing are wall, and the last rule, with no bounds, takes everything left: the far field. A face that matches no rule is an error, so end with a rule without bounds.

Reference values. reference_area is required in 3D: lift, drag and side force are per q_inf * reference_area. For a half model give the half model's area. reference_length and moment_centre are for the pitching moment: about the y axis through moment_centre, nose-up positive, per q_inf * reference_area * reference_length, pressure and friction together.

Reynolds number. Per unit length of the grid. The example grid has a root chord of 1, so 14.6e6 is the Reynolds number per root chord. Use coordinate_scale if your grid is in other units.

For Euler, leave out reynolds, material_properties and turbulence and make the wall a slip_wall.

docs.title: 3. numerical.json
docs.text:
{
    "convective_fluxes": {"riemann_solver": "hllc", "limiter": "van_albada"},
    "time_integration": {"solver": "implicit"},
    "implicit": {"max_relative_update": 0.2},
    "convergence": {"max_iters": 1500, "tol": 1e-12, "block_iters": 20}
}

van_albada is the robust choice with a shock. On coarse grids it costs accuracy: on the 135,168-cell level of this wing it gave a drag 21% above NASA's CFL3D on the same grid. CFL3D runs this case without a limiter and with the third-order upwind-biased reconstruction, which here is

"convective_fluxes": {"riemann_solver": "hllc", "limiter": "none", "muscl_kappa": 0.3333333333333333}

With it the same level is within 5.6% in drag and 0.8% in lift, and the 1,081,344-cell level within 1.74% and 0.19%. Without a limiter the residual can stall at a few orders while the forces are steady; judge by the forces.

docs.title: 4. Check the grid
docs.text:
jaxaero examples/onera_m6_sa --check

grid file om6_strct_16x44x24.ufmt: 1 block(s), 16896 cells, 1 body(ies); implicit, hllc, limiter van_albada
grid quality: 16896 cells, min area 1.84e-11, min angle 4.3 deg, max growth 5.42, ...; far field >= 98.3 from the walls
patch 'wall': no_slip_wall, 384 faces
patch 'farfield': far_field, 384 faces
patch 'symmetry': symmetry, 1056 faces
wall: 384 faces, x 0.0000 to 1.4147, y -0.0000 to 1.5012, z -0.0460 to 0.0460

Check that every patch you expect is there with a plausible number of faces, and that the wall's extent is the wing's, in the units of your Reynolds number. A seam or a pole does not appear: only the faces left for the rules do. (The skewness and growth warnings here come from this very coarse level at the tip.) There is no grid picture in 3D.

docs.title: 5. Run
docs.text:
jaxaero examples/onera_m6_sa

     200  res 4.5504e-05 ( 0.47 orders)  CL = +0.241207   CD = +0.040561 (friction +0.006224)   CM = -0.185453   CY = +0.001046
     300  res 7.5804e-06 ( 1.25 orders)  CL = +0.226177   CD = +0.039292 (friction +0.005443)   CM = -0.169032   CY = +0.000782
     460  res 2.9867e-08 ( 3.65 orders)  CL = +0.221072   CD = +0.038973 (friction +0.005306)   CM = -0.163561   CY = +0.000664
settled after 460 iterations, residual peak 1.343636e-04 -> 2.986654e-08 (3.65 orders from peak)

Three and a half minutes on a laptop GPU (4 GB), 0.33 s per step; the run stops once the forces have settled (section 6). CY is the side force. This level is far too coarse for the values to mean much (NASA's finest grids give CL 0.2693, CD 0.01696): it is there to try the workflow.

The result directory holds:

file content *_surface.dat one row per wall face: its indices i k on the wall, x y z, cp, and the skin-friction vector cf_x cf_y cf_z *_block0.vts the whole field for ParaView: density, velocity, pressure, Mach number per cell *_fields.npz the conservative state and the grid nodes *_residual.dat, *_lift.dat, *_metadata.json histories, the resolved case and provenance

python -m jaxaero.plot draws 2D results only. For a wing, python scripts/plot_wing.py RESULT_DIR draws the pressure on the upper and lower surfaces, with the sonic line, and a 3D view:

(The script assumes the layout of this grid family: the wall on j = 0, i along the span, k round the section from the leading edge.)

docs.title: 6. Cost
docs.text:
Measured on this wing (SA, case 2308), from freestream to settled forces:

cells device per step steps total 16,896 laptop GPU, 4 GB 0.33 s 460 3.5 min 135,168 A100 40 GB 0.13 s 1,560 4.5 min 1,081,344 A100 40 GB 1.32 s 2,520 57 min 1,081,344 CPU node, 24 cores 160 s (4.7 days at that rate)

The 8.65-million-cell level of the family does not fit on a 40 GB GPU.

Forces are steady after roughly 500 to 2500 steps, more on finer grids. The run stops there by itself (settled: CL, CD and CM each vary by less than convergence.forces_tol, 1e-4, over the last quarter of the iterations), or at tol or max_iters, whichever comes first; results are written at the end.

On a fine grid, "convergence": {"grid_sequencing": 1} (or 2, ...) solves first on the grid with every other node, and starts the case's grid from that solution: on the 1,081,344-cell level the forces settle within 1e-4 of their final values 2.8x sooner in fine-grid steps (620 against 1760). Every cell count, and every patch and interface limit, must stay even.

docs.title: 7. Finer grids of the example
docs.text:
NASA does not ship the ONERA M6 grids but the program that makes them. data/grids/README.md gives the recipe (two Fortran files, a few minutes) and the names of the levels: 135,168 and 1,081,344 cells are the ones NASA's reference results are quoted on. Point domain.file at a level, or

jaxaero examples/onera_m6_sa --set case.domain.file=data/grids/onera_m6/om6_strct_32x88x48.ufmt

docs.title: 8. Limits
docs.text:
• One block, Plot3D. No 3D grid generation, no multi-block 3D, no CGNS in 3D.
  • python -m jaxaero.plot and the --check picture are 2D only.
  • Polars (python -m jaxaero.polar) have not been tested in 3D.
  • The far field is plain characteristic (no point-vortex correction in 3D): put it far away, as here (100 chords).

docs.title: Design notes
docs.text: Why some things are done the way they are, with the measurements behind each choice, grouped by module.

docs.title: solvers/implicit.py
docs.text:
• Defect correction is the default Jacobian. On 112x32 over 400 steps, a limited second-order residual dropped 0.06 orders with the exact Jacobian and 2.8 with the first-order one; an unlimited residual gave 4.9 orders exact. The exact Jacobian of a limited scheme carries the limiter's kinks.
  • The CFL ramp keys off the linear solve, not the residual history. A stagnated GMRES returns a null update, which leaves the residual unchanged and looks like success to a residual-based test; a freestream start makes the residual rise through the transient, which looks like failure to textbook SER (Mulder and van Leer, J. Comput. Phys. 59 (1985)). One extra matvec, about 1% of a step, measures the linear reduction instead.
  • max_relative_update. Rejection alone only stops steps that leave the physical domain. On TMR NACA 0012 at 15 deg, 449x129, accepted steps built an odd-even checkerboard in nu~ and rho within 600 steps, after which every step was rejected; bounding the relative change (0.2) cured it.

docs.title: solvers/driver.py
docs.text:
• Force-based stopping is the default (convergence.forces_tol 1e-4, the gallery's settledness bar, applied to CL, CD and CM). On the M6 1.08M level from freestream it stops at 2540 steps with the forces within 3e-6 of the 3000-step values; 1e-5 did not stop within 3000 (the last-quarter window still holds the early drift). RANS residuals stall at round-off 10-11 orders down, and some cases at 2-3 (30P30N L1, NACA 0012 at 0 deg) with the forces settled to six digits long before. On RAE 2822 the run stops at 940 of 6000 steps with the 6000-step forces to every printed digit; on the M6 135k level at 1600, the same forces to six digits whatever the Krylov settings.

  • A frozen run stops as stalled, never settled. When every step is rejected the state does not move, so the forces are flat and would pass the settledness test (a mis-started 1.08M M6 run stopped as settled after 260 steps that way). A block whose residual is bitwise constant is no progress, whatever the equations.

  • Convergence is judged from the running peak. Started from uniform freestream, the first residual is near zero (every cell away from the wall is in equilibrium), so normalising by it reports a residual that appears to grow through the transient.

docs.title: core/config.py
docs.text:
• float64 only. A float32 path existed and was removed. The 5.9x double-precision penalty on a 4 GB laptop card is real, but every verification gate must run in double: a suite that cannot tell a bug from round-off is no use, and no result was ever quoted from the single-precision path.
  • HLLC by default: it resolves a stationary contact exactly and needs no entropy fix, so the scheme carries no tunable dissipation.
  • Krylov sizes. The Arnoldi loop (solvers/krylov.py) runs to full length whether or not it has converged, testing only between restarts, so a large subspace is paid in full every step: small subspace (10), two restarts. Inexact Newton tolerance 1e-2 (Eisenstat and Walker, SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 17 (1996)).
  • CFL ramp defaults. Start at 10 (five times what the explicit path tolerates); growth capped at 1.3 per step and earned by the residual reduction; cfl_max is a backstop, not a tuning knob: the ramp settles at whatever the preconditioner sustains, limited in practice by krylov_success.

docs.title: numerics/riemann.py
docs.text:
• Why HLLC. Roe's scheme is shock-unstable on high-aspect-ratio cells, and the TMR grids reach such ratios at the shock foot: on 448x128 at M 0.8 the transonic shock never settled (CL oscillating 0.04-0.28), curable only by an entropy-fix coefficient large enough to bias CL by 16%. HLLC takes its dissipation from wave-speed estimates, has no vanishing eigenvalue, and needs no fix. On the O-grid at M 0.8, alpha 1.25, 128 squared, the two agree to three digits (CL 0.33567 vs 0.33585, CD 0.025711 vs 0.025698, observed orders 0.94/1.37 vs 0.92/1.33), so Roe stays as the independent check, 15% cheaper per iteration.
  • Contact resolution is required: a slip wall has vn = 0 along its length, so a flux that smears contacts smears exactly where CL and CD are computed. A Rusanov entry was built and removed for that reason.

docs.title: numerics/reconstruction.py, numerics/limiters.py
docs.text:
• Raw index differences, not spacing-weighted gradients. Limiting a gradient over the real cell spacings is the formally correct second-order form on a graded grid; it was built, measured and removed. On the strongly graded TMR C-grids it lost badly (transonic CL 0.1854 against 0.2461, oscillation 4.5x larger): the TVD region of a limiter depends on the spacing ratio and these limiters ignore it. On the mildly graded conformal O-grids it lost marginally, for no gain in order (CD 0.003103 against 0.002831 at 128 squared, observed order 1.16 against 1.13). The weighted variant is in the git history.
  • Limiters take differences (a, b), not ratios: no 0/0 on a flat field, no guard epsilon. Every limiter must return exactly a at a == b (second order in smooth flow); this is unit-tested.
  • minmod vs van Albada. On the explicit path on TMR's C-grids minmod held a transonic shock where van Albada reached 2.29 orders against minmod's 4.39 (later confounded by those grids' own limit cycle). Van Albada came back for RAE 2822: smooth where active, close to the central slope in smooth flow. Van Leer is in the git history.
  • Venkatakrishnan is deliberately absent: it is a smooth Barth-Jespersen for unstructured grids, not a slope-ratio limiter; fed r = a/b it returns phi(1) = 3/4, quietly losing second order.

docs.title: mesh/coarsen.py
docs.text: • Grid sequencing coarsens the case's own grid (every other node, the segments' indices halved), so it needs no second grid file and works for generated, file and multi-block grids alike. Injection (each child takes its parent's value) is enough: from the settled 135k M6 level, the 1.08M level had its forces within 1e-4 of the 3000-step values for good from step 620, against 1760 from freestream. The canvas padding cells must keep the freestream start (a zero density there fails every step's physicality test).

docs.title: core/linalg.py
docs.text: • The line solve is block cyclic reduction, Thomas kept as the reference in the tests. A Thomas sweep is 2L dependent steps per application (L the chain length), each a small kernel: on an A100 the preconditioner was 89% of an RAE 2822 Newton step (121.7 against 13.6 ms with full-length GMRES). Odd-even reduction is ceil(log2 L) levels for about twice the flops: per apply 3.52 -> 0.136 ms on RAE 2822 (flow chains of 128), 2.08 -> 0.24 ms on M6 135k, and still faster at 1.08M cells (4.81 -> 2.89 ms) once the power-of-two padding was dropped (with it, 1.08M was no faster). lax.scan(unroll=8) gave only 2-4x and was dropped.

docs.title: solvers/krylov.py
docs.text: • Right preconditioning. On TMR's 112x32 C-grid at CFL 1000, ten left-preconditioned GMRES iterations returned a true residual 3.1x larger than they started with; ten right-preconditioned ones 0.47x (0.18x with the lines continued through the wake cut).

docs.title: mesh/atlas.py
docs.text: • Line chains stop at other blocks. Continued through every interface, 30P30N L1 ran 2.1x slower per step (chains of 190 cells instead of 66) for no convergence gain; only a block's own j-cut (the C-grid wake) is crossed.

docs.title: mesh/highlift.py, mesh/blocking.py (multi-element grids)
docs.text:
Measured on the 30P30N's elements at 150 wall cells per chord (75.9k cells main + flap, 113k all three), quality as tests/unit/test_highlift.py measures it.

  • One chain template, not three. An O-layer's outer contour is rounded at every trailing edge (and the 30P30N's are blunt), so a cut leaving the nose tip meets the contour tangentially: blocks cannot be split there. The families are compositions per element pair: a slot block over the downstream element (left side the gap cut and the upstream base, top the upstream wake), a cove block (upstream lip to base, gap cut, downstream nose, mouth), a drop from every lip. Fill blocks have j from a wall where they touch one.
  • The gap is a side, never a chain member. With the gap cut in the chain of one block over everything, 80 i-lines packed into the 0.005 gap ran up to the middle loop and Winslow's psi lost authority there (cells of 0.004-0.007 against 3e-4 wanted, 95x across the cut). As a side of both the cove and the slot it is 5-6x at worst, median 3.
  • Wakes are offsets of the slot's floor. A Hermite wake from a slat's trailing edge cannot follow the main element's surface; the floor (the downstream contour and wake) offset node for node, by the gap growing 10 % per unit length, does, and gives the slot straight near-normal lines. The normals are smoothed over two offsets and the curve over one, then the nodes put back at their arc fractions (averaging alone slid them: 12.7x at the main element's base); unsmoothed, the flap's base creased the main wake (17-24x across it).
  • Connectors fixed, each block smoothed alone. Smoothing all blocks at once with the connectors' nodes free (stencils across blocks) let corners collapse where three blocks meet (the slat cusp folded); anchoring the cuts' ends folded where anchored met free. Fixed Hermite cuts with spacing matched at their ends: no fold in any family.
  • Spacing control, iterated. Thomas-Middlecoff psi interpolated from a block's sides ignores the layer it sits on (first cells 10-20x the layer's last step mid-block). psi from the heights wanted off the bottom and top (per j line, from its end nodes alone) fixed the medians; three GRAPE-style rounds (heights rescaled by sqrt(wanted/got)) brought the concave-corner peak from 26.6x to 22.8x and medians to 1.1-1.4; more rounds skewed the cove and slot (12 rounds: 11 deg) and cost 100 s.
  • Near-wall layer. Hyperbolic marching folds into a concave corner (the main element's cove step) at any thickness above about a wall cell: its smoothing is raised 31x there, ramped from zero at the wall so the first steps stay normal; a residual fold halves the thickness round it and marches again. A sharp convex corner (the slat cusp, 18 deg) twisted its first cells until the corner's two neighbours were placed equally far (the step is normal to the chord through them). The march's smoothing at the wall tilted the first step 5-8 deg on the slat and main noses; from zero at the wall (except within two nodes of a convex corner, whose fan needs it) the wall is orthogonal to 0.05 deg. The first cell is re-marched until within 1 % of the wall spacing (up to 6 passes; the marching's area smoothing moved it 3-12 %).
  • Sharp trailing edges. A sharp trailing edge is the layer's seam node: the convex-corner test (heading jumps, unwrapped) missed it, the wall got no smoothing there and the layer folded, then was thinned to the floor and refused (every sharp main element with a flap). Turning is taken from each node's two edges instead, and the edge's two neighbours placed equally far, as at the slat cusp. NACA-based sections then build at 22-38 deg.
  • Targets not met yet. Smallest angle 20 deg: 17.4 deg at the main element's concave cove corner (one layer cell), 12.9 deg where the cove narrows into the flap gap (66 cells), 16.4 deg where the slot's left side turns from the gap cut onto the upstream base. Interface growth 1.3: 22.8x at the concave corner (the layer is thinned there and the cove's lines fan), 5-7x round the gap; medians 1.1-1.4. Tried and dropped: splitting the cove at its corner (to the downstream nose in proportion, or at its nearest point: slivers of 0.1-7.5 deg), and starting the slot where the channel narrows to three gaps (its left side then ran along the ceiling, parallel to its floor, and folded).

docs.title: 3D
docs.text:
• Face vectors from the diagonals' cross product, S = (x_c - x_a) x (x_d - x_b) / 2: the vector area of every surface the face's edges bound, so a cell's six vectors sum to zero exactly on warped faces and a collapsed face (a pole) is exactly zero. Volumes (1/3) sum S . x_f equal the trilinear hexahedron's (tested against Gauss quadrature).
  • Face gradients: the 2D diamond generalized (centre-to-centre vector plus the face's two diagonals, node values and positions both averaged from the 8 surrounding centres), not Green-Gauss on a dual cell: exact for linear fields on any hexahedra, the same property and code as 2D.
  • The pole is an interface, i_min facing itself half a turn round the O seam: the ghost across the axis is the diametrically opposite cell. Its faces have zero area, so it only feeds slopes and gradients.
  • Plane-reflection ghosts on skewed cells (walls, symmetry; 2D and 3D): the face state is off by O(h tan theta) on a cell skewed by theta, an O(1) local truncation error. Measured with the 3D MMS on a warped cube: first order in the solution with Dirichlet ghosts placed that way, second order with ghosts at the cells of linearly extrapolated nodes (a point reflection through the face midpoint). Kept for the physical conditions (standard; the M6 wall is within 2 deg of orthogonal except at the sharp trailing edge and the leading-edge seam); the MMS uses the latter.
  • 3D incidence is in x-z, span y (TMR's wing grids): freestream_primitive(flow, 3) is M (cos a, 0, sin a); a 2D grid extruded in z needs the freestream passed explicitly (tests/verification/test_extruded.py does).
